query: For refractory high-entropy alloys intended for structural use under extreme-temperature conditions, what single intervention could improve high-temperature oxygen resistance? State one hypothesis that identifies the intervention, explains its mechanism, predicts the improvement relative to the untreated alloy, defines the temperature, atmosphere, and exposure conditions under which it should work, cites supporting prior evidence, and proposes an experiment with a clear result that would falsify the hypothesis.

generation.hypothesis: A controlled boronizing treatment that creates a high-entropy boride surface layer will improve the high-temperature oxygen resistance of refractory high-entropy alloys compared to untreated alloys.
generation.material_initial_state: Refractory high-entropy alloys (RHEAs) in their untreated state, intended for structural applications under extreme-temperature conditions.
generation.intervention: Apply a controlled boronizing treatment to the surface of the RHEAs to form a protective high-entropy boride layer.
generation.conditions: Testing under oxidizing conditions at approximately 1300°C in air (or pure oxygen) for durations up to 100 hours.
generation.structural_mediator: The formation of a continuous, adherent high-entropy boride surface layer that acts as a barrier.
generation.mechanism: The boride layer is expected to be thermodynamically stable at high temperatures and to inhibit oxygen diffusion into the alloy. This barrier minimizes the rate and extent of oxide scale formation, thereby enhancing the alloy’s oxidation resistance.
generation.predicted_outcome: Compared to untreated RHEAs, those treated with the boronizing process will display a significantly reduced oxide scale thickness, lower weight gain due to oxidation, and better preservation of their mechanical integrity under high-temperature oxidizing conditions.
generation.baseline: Untreated refractory high-entropy alloys, which exhibit pronounced oxidation and substantial oxide scale growth under similar high-temperature exposure.
generation.boundary: The improvement is anticipated to be effective only under high-temperature oxidizing environments (above approximately 1200°C) where the boron diffusion and boride formation kinetics are favorable; results may vary if the temperature or oxygen partial pressure deviates significantly.
generation.uncertainty: The exact magnitude of the improvement in oxidation resistance and the long-term adhesion and stability of the surface boride layer are uncertain and require further experimental validation.

falsification_experiment.design: Prepare two groups of RHEA samples: one group undergoes the controlled boronizing treatment and the other remains untreated as control. Expose both groups to an oxidizing environment at 1300°C in air for 100 hours.
measurements: Oxide scale thickness using cross-sectional scanning electron microscopy (SEM)
Surface phase composition via X-ray diffraction (XRD) and energy-dispersive X-ray spectroscopy (EDS)
Weight gain measurements to quantify oxidation
falsification_experiment.falsification_rule: The hypothesis will be falsified if the boronized samples do not show a statistically significant reduction in oxide scale thickness, weight gain, or if the presence of a protective boride layer is not confirmed compared to the untreated samples.

cited_evidence.text: High-entropy alloys (HEAs) represent a new class of alloys that consist of more than four alloying elements in close to equiatomic concentrations (). The diverse compositional possibilities of HEAs, combined with appropriate heat treatment conditions, offer the potential to develop new alloys with a combination of remarkable properties such as outstanding mechanical properties, high-hydrogen absorption capacity, and robust resistance to corrosion and radiation (). The refractory HEAs (RHEAs) based on refractory elements were proposed by Senkov et al. () as a new class of high-temperature structural alloys that might surpass the capabilities of nickel-based superalloys. RHEAs are emerging as prominent contenders in diverse industries, notably in the nuclear and aerospace sectors (, ).

The presence of intermetallic compounds, such as brittle Laves phases, typically reduces the ductility of RHEAs (), prompting extensive efforts to develop single-phase RHEAs for high-temperature applications (, , , , , , ). The equiatomic Ti-V-Nb-Ta alloy is one of the most attractive RHEAs, which solidifies as a single-phase body-centered cubic (BCC) microstructure with heterogeneous elemental distribution and exhibits excellent high-temperature strength and room-temperature ductility (). Equimolar Ti-V-Nb-Ta has an extremely high compressive yield strength, 1273 MPa at room temperature and 688 MPa at 900°C (). By comparison, conventional high-temperature Ni-base superalloys notably soften above 600°C, with the compressive yield strength dropping to ~200 MPa at 900°C (). Equimolar Ti-V-Nb-Ta also exhibits impressive tensile ductility, ~14% at room temperature (), and a relatively low brittle-to-ductile transition temperature between −47° and −27°C, comparable to BCC metals and stainless steels for engineering applications (, ). In this work, the formation of carbide with the concertation of carbon at 0.1 at.% in refractory high-entropy alloy (RHEA) Mo15Nb20Re15Ta30W20 was studied under both ambient and high-pressure high-temperature conditions. The x-ray diffraction of dilute carbon (C)-doped RHEA under ambient pressure showed that the phases and lattice constant of RHEA were not influenced by the addition of 0.1 at.% C. In contrast, C-doped RHEA showed unexpected phase formation and transformation under combined high-pressure and high-temperature conditions by resistively employing the heated diamond anvil cell (DAC) technique. The new FCC_L12 phase appeared at 6 GPa and 809 °C and preserved the ambient temperature and pressure. High-pressure and high-temperature promoted the formation of carbides Ta3C and Nb3C, which are stable and may further improve the mechanical performance of the dilute C-doped alloy Mo15Nb20Re15Ta30W20.

reading.lever: Apply a controlled boronizing treatment to form a protective high-entropy boride surface layer.
reading.why: This lever draws upon the proven oxidation resistance of high-entropy boride materials, suggesting that a surface coating approach could enhance high-temperature oxygen resistance in RHEAs.
